name: The Twisted Beech of Square des Arenes de Lutece

location.address: Square des Arenes de Lutece, 2 Place Emile Male, 75005 Paris
location.neighbourhood: Latin Quarter, next to the Roman arena, 5th arrondissement

verified_sources: Ville de Paris arbres remarquables register (register_id 132669.0, girth 110cm, Square des arenes de Lutece)
access: Free, public square, open daily (closes in the evening per standard Paris square hours)
transport: Jussieu (Metro 7/10) or Place Monge (Metro 7), 4-5 min walk
verify_notes: A hetre tortillard (also called a 'fau', old French for beech), a naturally occurring twisted-branch variant of the common European beech whose only wild population in the world is the Faux de Verzy forest near Reims, about 1,000 specimens. This is a grafted/planted specimen, not a wild one. Sources describe it as planted around 1905, which lines up with the register's registered status as a mature designated tree. Register girth 110cm at last measurement, no height given by the register; independent descriptions call it short and umbrella-shaped rather than tall, consistent with the species' known dwarf, sprawling growth form (never reads as a data error the way a girth would). In winter its 'tormented architecture' shows: trunk and branches twisted, bent and spiraling, some branches trailing to the ground; in summer it disappears under a dense, low, rounded canopy. Sits inside the Square des Arenes de Lutece, the garden built around Paris's excavated 1st-century Roman amphitheatre (arena capacity originally ~15,000), rediscovered during 19th-century boulevard works and partly saved after a campaign that Victor Hugo joined. The tree itself has no connection to the Roman ruins beyond sharing the same small garden, so the story should keep the two hooks separate: Roman arena as the site's history, twisted beech as the tree's own oddity. Extends the existing Jussieu/Latin Quarter cluster: about 300m from the Jardin des Plantes trio (par_002/003/004) and roughly 700m-1km from Square Samuel Paty (par_013) and Square Michel-Foucault (par_014), all walkable together. No news of removal or damage found; square appears in current listings as an active public garden.

name: The Anne Frank Chestnut

location.address: Jardin Anne Frank, 14 Impasse Berthaud, 75003 Paris

verified_sources: Ville de Paris arbres remarquables register (register_id 134435.0, girth 100cm, Jardin Anne Franck)
access: Free, public garden, open daily (standard Paris square hours)
transport: Rambuteau (Metro 11) or Chatelet-Les Halles, 4-5 min walk
verify_notes: This is young by this project's usual bar (planted 2007, about 19 years old) and qualifies on historical/symbolic significance rather than age, same test as the Elm of Saint-Gervais (par_007). It is a graft grown from the horse chestnut tree Anne Frank could see and wrote about from the attic window of the Secret Annex in Amsterdam; that original Amsterdam tree was itself centuries old, ill with fungal and moth damage for years, and finally fell in a storm in August 2010, three years after this graft was planted. Officially classified by the Ville de Paris as an 'arbre remarquable' specifically for its symbolic value, not its size, which the register itself allows for. Planted 20 June 2007 in a formal ceremony with mayor Bertrand Delanoe and Hans Westra, then director of the Anne Frank House Amsterdam, the same year the garden (on the grounds of the 17th-century Hotel de Saint-Aignan, now the Musee d'art et d'histoire du Judaisme) was inaugurated. One independent source (detoursmag, not included above as it could not be re-fetched to double check this pass, but consistent with pariszigzag) gives circumference 72cm at 8m height; the register (fetched 2026-08-05) gives 100cm, a plausible ~13 years of subsequent growth on a young, vigorous chestnut rather than a conflict, but flag the discrepancy for the writer rather than picking one figure silently. Garden itself has a Holocaust memorial character: a boy and girl's names inscribed at the entrance in memory of the 11,000 Jewish children deported from France. Distance from the existing cluster: about 700m from Square Saint-Gervais (par_007, 48.85536,2.3527), an easy walkable extension north into the Marais rather than a standalone.

name: The Fig Tree of Square Georges Cain
age_estimate: over a century (no exact planting date documented)

location.address: Square Georges Cain, 8 Rue Payenne, 75003 Paris
location.neighbourhood: Le Marais, next to the Musee Carnavalet, 3rd arrondissement

verified_sources: Ville de Paris arbres remarquables register (register_id 116020.0, girth 145cm, height 10m, Square Georges Cain)
access: Free, public square, open daily (standard Paris square hours)
transport: Saint-Paul (Metro 1) or Chemin Vert (Metro 8), 4-6 min walk
verify_notes: No exact planting date found in any source checked; multiple independent write-ups (pariszigzag ran at least two separate features on this square) call the fig 'over a hundred years old' / 'century-old' and officially classified remarkable, consistently with the register's own designation, but nobody names a year, so this pass could not pin an age range the way it did for the beech (par_016). Register gives girth 145cm and height 10m, both plausible for an old open-grown fig, which can live centuries in a sheltered courtyard setting; figs are shorter-lived and more cold-sensitive than most trees on this list, so 10m/145cm at open exposure in Paris is itself notable and part of why it earned the remarkable-tree label. Square Georges Cain (created 1923, 2,128 sqm) is a small, quiet open-air lapidary garden for the neighbouring Musee Carnavalet: architectural fragments, statues (including a Maillol bronze) and stonework from demolished Paris buildings are scattered through the planting, on the site of medieval market gardens (culture Sainte-Catherine) that predate the square by centuries, which is a good scene-setting hook distinct from the tree's own age claim. Flagged rather than delivered as clean-verified because the 'over a century' age is a repeated but undated claim, not a sourced planting year; the writer should phrase it as descriptive rather than precise. About 800m from Square Saint-Gervais (par_007) and roughly 1.2km from the Rene-Viviani/Saint-Gervais core, at the edge of the brief's 1.5km radius, in the Marais rather than the Latin Quarter side of the cluster.
